The Graph Engineering Revolution in AI: DeerFlow 2.0, Claude Code and the End of Isolated Agents!

The video explains the difference between loop engineering, in which an agent decides his own path, and graph engineering, in which the paths and passages of work are defined in the code. Then shows how DeerFlow 2.0 applies this with subagents, on-demand skills and a sandbox for agents to work.

  • Data and decision-making

From chat to stream automation

AI agents stopped being chat assistants and started automating complex workflows 00:00. For this to work without the system hallucinating or locking, the software design had to change 00:00.

Loop Engineering

The problem is to get AI to solve complex tasks without losing process control 01:04. When a single agent does a long task from start to finish, the chance of him getting lost is great. 01:04.

In loop engineering, a single agent runs a continuous cycle until the problem is solved. Whoever develops sets the goal, and the path stays with the agent 01:24. The cycle usually has five steps: finding out what you need, planning, performing, checking your own work and correcting 01:47. If wrong, the agent restarts the cycle alone 02:10.

Graph Engineering: the organogram

The video uses an analogy: the loop is a generalist professional who tries to solve everything himself; the graph is the organization chart of a company, in which the developer defines the paths and passages of responsibility 02:30.

A graph has three parts 02:50:

  • We: experts, who perform the work 02:50.
  • Edges: say where the work goes next, in sequence or in parallel 02:50.
  • Shared status: the collective memory of the system 03:12.

When to use each

If the task is linear and has a clear end, the loop suffices 03:32. If you need to divide the task, rotate parts in parallel and pass the work formally, the graph is better 03:32. In the graph, each node can use a different model and tool, and a failure is isolated 03:53.

The rule is to dominate the loop first. The graph is an architecture pattern, not a magic solution: use it only when control and parallelism justify 03:53. The starting point should be the most simple and cheaper loop 04:15.

DeerFlow 2.0

According to the video, DeerFlow has almost 80,000 stars on GitHub. 04:37. Version 2 came first on GitHub Trending on February 28, 2026, and the tool went from deep research to orchestration platform 04:57.

DeerFlow does not depend on a template: you can use DeepSeek, OpenAI or Gemini 05:17. It is open source, with MIT license, integrates with Slack and Telegram and can be extended by MCP protocol 05:39.

Subagents and skills

The lead agent acts like a manager. It creates subagents on demand, but only when there is clear gain, how to rotate actions in parallel or isolate the context 06:00.

Skills are slowly loaded, only when asked, which keeps the context clean and saves tokens 06:22. Already come skills for deep search, code, slides, web pages, images and videos 06:43. As are Markdown files, any skill can be created or exchanged 07:03.

A computer for agents

DeerFlow gives agents an isolated sandbox, which can run in a Docker container or Kubernetes 07:24. There the agent has browser, terminal and real files, and can work for hours without leaving isolation 07:24.

The agent reads files, runs commands on the shell, tests the code he wrote and fixes errors 07:44. There is also integration with Claude Code in the terminal to send tasks and accompany the subagents 08:05.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I start with a loop or a graph?

With a loop. The graph is only worth it when the task asks for control and parallelism 04:15.

Does DeerFlow force you to use a specific model?

Nope. It works with various suppliers such as DeepSeek, OpenAI and Gemini 05:17.

About the video

In this video, we dive deep into the future of artificial intelligence architecture and the historical transition that is happening in the developer community: the evolution of Loop Engineering to Graph Engineering.
If you have already frustrated yourself with self-employed agents that "lost the course" in long tasks or want to understand how to build predictable and scalable multiagent systems, this content is indispensable.
We explore DeerFlow 2.0, ByteDance's powerful open source framework for deep-search and coding long-term tasks
, and we analyze the innovative deer-workflow pilot project (DeerWork), which establishes the basis for the DeerFlow 3.0, bringing orchestration entirely to TypeScript and delegating semantic work to replaceable agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pi.
What you will learn in this video:
Loop vs. Graph Engineering: Discover the fundamental difference between leaving an agent free to choose your own path in a loop or declaring explicit paths, edges and checks using agent graphs.
The Metaphor of the Organogram: Why agents are no longer being "generalists" who do everything themselves to work on structures with defined roles and data hands-offs.
DeerFlow 2.0 Anatomy: The role of sandboxes Safe Docker, short-term persistent memory and integrated message gateways with Telegram, Slack and Lark
.
Dynamic Workflow Runtime: How to use TypeScript as the deterministic execution plan of your system, using primitive flow as parallel(), pipeline() and phase().
Orchestration of Replaceable Agents: Like Claude Code, Codex and Pi act as plugable and modular semantic gears under a unified and neutral supplier interface.
